Handwriting
HAND-rye-ting
n. (a written bond; a signed certificate of debt)
Greek cheirographon, literally a thing written by hand — in the commercial Greek of the first century, a signed note of indebtedness, an IOU acknowledged by the debtor's own hand. The Authorized Version keeps the concrete legal image rather than softening it to record or charge.

Biblical Definition

Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross. Paul reaches for a debtor's bond, and the choice of image is the whole argument. A handwriting is not an accusation made by an enemy; it is a document the debtor himself signed. The law of God, holy and just and good, stood against us not because it was unjust but because we had subscribed to it and failed it, and the bond was in force. Two things are said of that bond, and both are decisive. It was against us — legally valid, properly drawn, enforceable. And it was contrary to us — actively opposed, standing in the way of every approach to God. Paul does not say the bond was cancelled by divine leniency, nor that God overlooked it, nor that it was discovered to be invalid. He says it was blotted out, taken out of the way, and nailed to the cross. The debt was not waived; it was transferred and discharged in the body of Christ, who having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances, made peace. This is why there is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus. The bond is not in a drawer somewhere, suspended. It is nailed up, publicly, spent.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): the cast or form of writing peculiar to each hand or person; a writing; anything written; that which is written by hand.

expand to see more

HANDWRITING, n. The cast or form of writing peculiar to each hand or person.

HANDWRITING, n. Anything written by hand; a writing; that which has been written.

BOND, n. An obligation or deed by which a person binds himself, his heirs, executors and administrators, to pay a certain sum on or before a future day appointed.

ORDINANCE, n. A rule established by authority; a permanent rule of action; a law or statute.

BLOT, v.t. To obliterate writing with ink; to efface; to erase; to cause to be unseen or forgotten.

Key Scripture

Colossians 2:14 — "Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross;"

Ephesians 2:15 — "Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances; for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace;"

Galatians 3:13 — "Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree:"

Romans 8:1 — "There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit."

Modern Corruption

Modern preaching regularly reduces the handwriting to a feeling of guilt and the blotting out to a change in how we see ourselves; Scripture makes it a real legal instrument really discharged by a real death.

expand to see more

The therapeutic retelling of Colossians 2:14 makes the bond subjective — the accusing voice in a believer's head, the shame he carries, the internalized critic — and makes the cross a demonstration that God never really held anything against him. That is a different gospel with the same vocabulary. Paul's bond is objective, and God is the party who holds it. The cross does not tell us the debt was imaginary; it tells us the debt was paid. A man comforted by being told he never owed anything has not been forgiven, and the moment his conscience wakes he will find the comfort empty, because the bond he actually signed is untouched.

The opposite corruption keeps the legal language but relocates the payment into the believer's own obedience, so that the bond is blotted out progressively as the Christian improves. Rome's system of merit and satisfaction does exactly this, and every revivalist scheme that makes assurance ride on performance does it again in Protestant dress. The text will not bear it. The blotting out, the taking out of the way, and the nailing are all in the aorist — done, finished, at a point in past time, by another. The believer contributes the debt. Christ contributes the payment.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek cheirographon (G5498), a handwritten bond; exaleipho (G1813), to wipe out or blot out; dogma (G1378), decree or ordinance; proseloo (G4338), to nail to.

expand to see more

Greek cheirographon (G5498) — a bond written by the debtor's own hand; rendered handwriting at Colossians 2:14, its only occurrence.

Greek exaleipho (G1813) — to wipe away, to blot out utterly; used of blotting out sins and of blotting a name out of the book of life.

Greek dogma (G1378) — a decree or ordinance; the ordinances the bond consisted of.

Greek proseloo (G4338) — to fasten with nails; used only here, of the bond nailed to the cross.

Greek hupenantios (G5227) — set over against, opposed; rendered contrary to us.

Usage

"“the handwriting of ordinances that was against us” — the bond, valid and enforceable."

"“took it out of the way” — removed from the middle, where it had blocked the way to God."

"“nailing it to his cross” — the discharged bond posted publicly, as a receipt."
